'''Joachim Wilhelm "Jo" Messing''' (September 10, 1946 – September 13, 2019) was a German-American biologist who was a professor of molecular biology and the fourth director of the [[Waksman Institute of Microbiology]] at [[Rutgers University]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waksman.rutgers.edu/about_waksman.php |title=The Waksman Institute homepage |publisher=Waksman.rutgers.edu |accessdate=2010-11-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100708051426/http://waksman.rutgers.edu/about_waksman.php |archivedate=2010-07-08 }}</ref>

Upon his arrival at Rutgers in 1985, Jo Messing initiated research activity on computational and structural biology and further emphasis on molecular genetics of the regulation of gene expression and biomolecular interactions.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waksman.rutgers.edu/about_history.php |title=The History of the Waksman Institute of Microbiology |publisher=Waksman.rutgers.edu |accessdate=2010-11-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100708095208/http://waksman.rutgers.edu/about_history.php |archivedate=2010-07-08 }}</ref> In the eighties, he provided incubator space for two Biotechnology centers at Rutgers, one in Medicine and one in Agriculture.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waksman.rutgers.edu/docs/ar2007.pdf |title=The Waksman Institute's Annual Report 2006–2007 |accessdate=2010-11-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100709205601/http://waksman.rutgers.edu/docs/ar2007.pdf |archivedate=2010-07-09 }}</ref> Subsequently, he also founded two new departments at Rutgers and served as the first chair, the Department of Molecular Biology and Biochemistry and the Department of Genetics.

Messing was also involved in the Plant Genome Initiative at Rutgers, which has contributed to the sequencing of the maize, [[sorghum]], and the rice genome.<ref>[http://www.maizegenome.org/ Maize genome.org, A Website about Maize Genome Sequencing Projects]</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://lifesci.rutgers.edu/~molbiosci/faculty/messing.html |title=Graduate programs in Molecular Biosciences at Rutgers |publisher=Lifesci.rutgers.edu |date= |accessdate=2010-11-10}}</ref> Besides maize, sorghum, and rice, they have also contributed to the sequencing of the Brachypodium<ref>{{cite journal |author=International Brachypodium Initiative |title=Genome sequencing and analysis of the model grass Brachypodium distachyon. |journal=Nature |volume=463|issue=7282 |pages=763–8 |date=February 11, 2010 |pmid=20148030 |doi=10.1038/nature08747|bibcode=2010Natur.463..763T |doi-access=free }}</ref> and Spirodela genomes.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Wang W, Messing J |title=The Spirodela polyrhiza genome reveals insights into its neotenous reduction fast growth and aquatic lifestyle. |journal=Nature Communications |volume=5|issue=3311 |pages=3311 |date=February 19, 2014 |pmid=24548928 |pmc=3948053 |doi= 10.1038/ncomms4311 |doi-access= free|bibcode=2014NatCo...5.3311W }}</ref>

Messing died at his home in [[Somerset, New Jersey]] on September 13, 2019, three days after his 73rd birthday.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2019/09/27/science/joachim-messing-dead.html|title = Joachim Messing, 73, Who Charted the DNA of Viruses and Plants, Dies|work = [[The New York Times]]|last = Sheikh|first = Knvul|date = September 27, 2019|accessdate = September 27, 2019}}</ref>

== Research ==
Jo Messing was a pharmacist by training, but specialized in molecular biology during his PhD-research at [[LMU Munich]] and the [[Max-Planck Institute]] of Biochemistry.

In the late seventies and early eighties, Jo Messing and his colleagues developed the shotgun DNA sequencing method with single and paired synthetic universal primers. The method is based on fragmenting DNA into small sizes, purifying them by cloning, and defining the start of sequencing with a short oligonucleotide.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Messing J, Crea R, Seeburg PH |title=A system for shotgun DNA sequencing |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=309–21 |date=January 1981 |pmid=6259625 |pmc=326694 |doi=10.1093/nar/9.2.309}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vieira J, Messing J |title=The pUC plasmids, an M13mp7-derived system for insertion mutagenesis and sequencing with synthetic universal primers |journal=Gene |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=259–68 |date=October 1982 |pmid=6295879 |doi=10.1016/0378-1119(82)90015-4}}</ref> Because fragmentation produces overlapping fragments, sequences can be concatenated by overlapping sequence information,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Larson R, Messing J |title=Apple II software for M13 shotgun DNA sequencing |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=39–49 |date=January 1982 |pmid=6278410 |pmc=326112 |doi=10.1093/nar/10.1.39}}</ref> thereby reconstructing contiguous sequences (contigs), which was first exemplified by the complete structure of a plant DNA virus.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Gardner RC, Howarth AJ, Hahn P, Brown-Luedi M, Shepherd RJ, Messing J |title=The complete nucleotide sequence of an infectious clone of cauliflower mosaic virus by M13mp7 shotgun sequencing |journal=Nucleic Acids Research |volume=9 |issue=12 |pages=2871–88 |date=June 1981 |pmid=6269062 |pmc=326899 |doi=10.1093/nar/9.12.2871}}</ref> His cloning vectors were also used to develop the method for oligonucleotide site-directed mutagenesis.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Norrander J, Kempe T, Messing J |title=Construction of improved M13 vectors using oligodeoxynucleotide-directed mutagenesis |journal=Gene |volume=26 |issue=1 |pages=101–6 |date=December 1983 |pmid=6323249 |doi=10.1016/0378-1119(83)90040-9}}</ref> [[DNA cloning]], [[shotgun sequencing]] and site-directed mutagenesis became widely used to sequence large DNA molecules like human chromosomes and to engineer genes and proteins. These methods are freely available, have been the cornerstone of the biotechnology industry and are cited in many patents.

At Rutgers, his plant genetics initiatives were directed towards the evolution of plant chromosomes and gene duplication. He also did research in [[non-Mendelian inheritance]]. Applied research in these genomic sequences permitted his laboratory to study the organization and evolution of the genes that control the supply of proteins for nutrition and as sources of biofuel. Projects with [[maize]] focused on upgrading the nutritional value of corn by genetically modifying corn to make [[methionine]] and lysine in the seeds, two [[essential amino acid]]s that people and livestock need in their diet. Investigating the genetic properties of [[sorghum]] led to a natural sorghum variant with increased sugar in the stem allows the plant to be used for both [[biofuel]] and feed. Most recent initiatives investigating the properties of spirodela ([[duckweed]]) led to its discovery as an alternative bio-energy source.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waksman.rutgers.edu/waks/messing/messing.html |title=Messing's personal website at the Waksman Institute |publisher=Waksman.rutgers.edu |accessdate=2010-11-10 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101206103020/http://waksman.rutgers.edu/Waks/Messing/messing.html |archivedate=2010-12-06 }}</ref>

== Education ==
* 1968: B.S. in Pharmacy, Düsseldorf, Germany
* 1971: M.S. in Pharmacy, [[Free University of Berlin]], Berlin
* 1975: [[Dr. rer. nat.]] in Biochemistry/Pharmacy, [[LMU Munich]], Munich, Germany<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hcr3.isiknowledge.com/author.cgi?id=384&cb=20 |title=Jo Messing, Highly cited scientist in ISI web of Knowledge.com |publisher=Hcr3.isiknowledge.com |date=2003-08-20 |accessdate=2010-11-10}}</ref>

== Professional career ==
* 1975–1978: Research Fellow, [[Max Planck Institute]] of Biochemistry, Munich, Germany
* 1978–1980: Research Associate in Bacteriology, [[University of California]], Davis, CA
* 1980–1982: Assistant Professor of Biochemistry, [[University of Minnesota]], St. Paul, MN
* 1982–1984: Associate Professor of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN
* 1984–1985: Professor of Biochemistry, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN
* 1985–2019: University Professor of Molecular Biology, Rutgers University
* 1988–2019: Director, Waksman Institute, Rutgers University
